sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses abuse, neglect, the drugging of residents and deaths in nursing homes. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the TTI
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Nursing homes are not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track nursing homes or assisted living facilities. The overlap between the two is smaller than it is for foster care or psychiatric hospitals. It is real in a few places: the same investors, the use of drugs to control behavior, an inspection system with the same weaknesses, and younger disabled people who end up in nursing homes.

We are not experts on long-term care. Residents, their families, ombudsmen and the organizations listed below have done this work for decades. Please learn from them first.

sections.label: What the industry is
sections.heading: What nursing homes are
sections.body:
A nursing home (in Medicare's terms, a skilled nursing facility) gives 24-hour nursing care to people who need help with daily life or are recovering after a hospital stay. As of July 2025 there were [14,742 nursing homes certified by CMS and about 1.24 million people living in them](https://www.kff.org/medicaid/a-look-at-nursing-facility-characteristics/). Residents received an average of 3.85 hours of nursing care a day, most of it from nurse aides, and 27 percent of homes were cited for serious deficiencies that caused harm or put a resident in immediate jeopardy.

**Who owns them.** In 2025, [73 percent of certified nursing homes were for-profit](https://www.kff.org/other-health/state-indicator/nursing-facilities-by-ownership-type/), 20 percent non-profit and 7 percent government-owned. The GAO estimated that [about 5 percent had private equity owners in 2022](https://www.kff.org/medicaid/a-look-at-nursing-facility-characteristics/), and said the federal data could not show the full number.

**Who pays.** Medicaid is the main payer for [63 percent of residents and Medicare for 14 percent](https://www.kff.org/medicaid/a-look-at-nursing-facility-characteristics/). In 2023 Medicaid paid 44 percent of the cost of long-term institutional care, and residents and families paid 37 percent out of pocket.

**What private equity ownership did.** A study of Medicare patients by Atul Gupta, Sabrina Howell, Constantine Yannelis and Abhinav Gupta, [first released in 2021 and published in 2024](https://www.nber.org/papers/w28474), found that private equity ownership of a nursing home raised patients' mortality by about 11 percent. Nurse staffing fell after the buyouts, and the authors name this as one reason for the deaths.

### Assisted living

Assisted living facilities (residential care communities) house people who cannot live on their own but do not need a nursing home's skilled care. In 2022 there were [about 32,200 of them with 988,800 residents, and 81.5 percent were for-profit](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/fastats/residential-care-communities.htm). States license them. Medicaid pays for some of their care: [48 states spent over $10 billion on it in 2014](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-18-179).

sections.label: Where it meets the TTI
sections.heading: Where it meets the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
### Shared roots

The two systems share a starting point. In the almshouses Dorothea Dix investigated from the 1840s, [children, elderly people and people with mental illness were confined together](/orphanages/); reformers moved the children out into orphanages and other institutions of their own, which our history treats as one of the roots of the troubled teen industry. Medicaid, created in 1965, became the main payer for most nursing home residents, and the same Medicaid money began paying for [private residential placements of children](/birth-of-the-tti/), including children with developmental disabilities ([our timeline](/idd-timeline/)).

### The same investors

The Canadian buyout firm Onex has owned both. In 2005 it bought [Skilled Healthcare Group, then the operator of 70 nursing and assisted living homes](https://www.ocbj.com/news/skilled-healthcare-sold-to-onex/) in California, Texas, Nevada and Kansas. Onex took a stake in ResCare in 2004 and [bought the rest of the company in 2010](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/776325/000095012310084472/y86520exv99w1.htm). ResCare's [own filings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000776325/000110465912010518/a11-30009_110k.htm) describe serving "young people with emotional and behavioral issues" and "juveniles in the justice system" in residential treatment facilities, group homes and foster care. ResCare [was renamed BrightSpring Health](https://homehealthcarenews.com/2018/09/pe-firm-onex-reportedly-exploring-sale-of-brightspring-formerly-rescare/) in 2018. Two West Virginia programs under the ResCare name are in our records. Skilled Healthcare [merged into Genesis HealthCare in 2015](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001351051/000110465915037232/a15-10889_2ex99d1.htm), and in 2021 Onex [bought a majority of Newport Healthcare](https://bhbusiness.com/2021/07/20/onex-partners-finalizes-60-purchase-of-newport-in-reported-1-3b-deal/), the owner of Newport Academy ([our corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)).

Onex bought Newport from the Carlyle Group, which had [invested in Newport Academy by 2017](https://bhbusiness.com/2021/04/14/carlyle-group-reportedly-considering-sale-of-teen-rehab-company-newport-academy/). Carlyle had owned HCR ManorCare, one of the largest nursing home chains, [since 2007](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/amp/wbna19548445) and [lost its stake](https://insurancenewsnet.com/oarticle/judge-approves-hcr-manorcare-bankruptcy-plan) when ManorCare [went bankrupt in 2018](https://financierworldwide.com/hcr-manorcare-enters-bankruptcy), owing $7.1 billion.

Real estate investment trusts such as Sabra and CareTrust own nursing homes and have [moved into adult addiction treatment](https://bhbusiness.com/2022/11/18/reits-could-be-a-knight-in-shining-armor-for-behavioral-health-investors-and-operators/). We did not find a trust or private equity firm that we could document owning both nursing homes and youth residential programs today. If you know of one, please tell us.

### Drugs used to control behavior

Using a drug to make a person easier to manage, rather than to treat a condition, is called chemical restraint. In nursing homes the drugs are mostly antipsychotics given to people with dementia. Human Rights Watch found in 2018 that in an average week, nursing homes gave antipsychotics to [over 179,000 people who did not have a diagnosis the drugs are approved for](https://www.hrw.org/report/2018/02/05/they-want-docile/how-nursing-homes-united-states-overmedicate-people-dementia). CMS's [National Partnership to Improve Dementia Care](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/data-show-national-partnership-improve-dementia-care-achieves-goals-reduce-unnecessary-antipsychotic), started in 2012, lowered the reported rate among long-stay residents from 23.9 to 15.7 percent by early 2017. That measure leaves out residents diagnosed with schizophrenia, and in 2026 the HHS Inspector General found that nursing homes had [given residents schizophrenia diagnoses to hide their use of antipsychotics](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2026/nursing-homes-inappropriately-diagnosed-residents-with-schizophrenia-to-mask-the-misuse-of-antipsychotic-drugs).

The Senate Finance Committee's 2024 investigation of youth residential treatment facilities run by Universal Health Services, Acadia Healthcare, Devereux and Vivant has a section on [chemical restraint and polypharmacy](https://www.finance.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/sfc_report_warehouses_of_neglect.pdf) among the harms it documented ([our summary of the report](/warehouses-of-neglect/)).

### Inspections that miss what happens

Nursing homes are inspected by state survey agencies under contract with CMS, and the results are published on [Care Compare](https://www.medicare.gov/care-compare/). CMS puts the homes with the worst records in its Special Focus Facility program, which has limited places. Until 2019 the roughly 400 homes that qualified but were not selected [were kept hidden from the public](https://www.aging.senate.gov/press-releases/casey-toomey-secure-cms-commitment-to-publicly-release-monthly-list-of-underperforming-nursing-facilities-).

Nursing homes may ask residents to sign arbitration agreements, which send disputes to a private arbitrator instead of a court. A [2019 federal rule](https://www.agg.com/news-insights/publications/cms-finalizes-rules-on-nursing-home-arbitration-agreements/) allows these agreements but bars making them a condition of admission or of continued care.

### Younger disabled people

In *Olmstead v. L.C.* (1999) the Supreme Court held that the Americans with Disabilities Act [prohibits the unjustified segregation of people with disabilities](https://www.ada.gov/resources/olmstead-mandate-statement/) and requires community services where they are appropriate and the person does not oppose them. Nursing homes still house many disabled people under 65. A 2022 study found they were [more likely than older residents to live in for-profit and lower-quality homes](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36190884/), and that in many states the rate of placement of younger people stayed flat or grew while it fell for older adults. We have not found figures on how many young people move from youth programs into nursing homes.

sections.label: What investigations found
sections.heading: What investigations have found
sections.body:
- **Abuse citations doubled (GAO, 2019).** Nursing home deficiencies for abuse rose [from 430 in 2013 to 875 in 2017](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-433), with the largest increase among the most severe. Staff were more often the abusers than anyone else. CMS did not check whether state agencies referred abuse cases to law enforcement.
- **Abuse that was not reported (HHS-OIG, 2019).** The Inspector General estimated that [one in five high-risk emergency room claims](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2019/incidents-of-potential-abuse-and-neglect-at-skilled-nursing-facilities-were-not-always-reported-and-investigated/) for nursing home residents in 2016 came from potential abuse or neglect. Nursing homes failed to report many of these incidents to the state, as federal rules require.
- **Drugging people with dementia (Human Rights Watch, 2018).** ["They Want Docile"](https://www.hrw.org/report/2018/02/05/they-want-docile/how-nursing-homes-united-states-overmedicate-people-dementia) found antipsychotics often given without free and informed consent, as a chemical restraint for staff convenience or to discipline residents.
- **False diagnoses (HHS-OIG, 2026).** Reviewing inspections of 40 nursing homes, the Inspector General found that [medical directors made inappropriate schizophrenia diagnoses](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2026/nursing-homes-inappropriately-diagnosed-residents-with-schizophrenia-to-mask-the-misuse-of-antipsychotic-drugs) to justify antipsychotics and to get around Medicare safeguards.
- **Hidden ownership (GAO, 2023).** Care Compare [did not let families see which homes shared an owner](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-23-104813) or how that owner's homes performed. CMS added common ownership information in June 2023.
- **Assisted living (GAO, 2018).** [26 state Medicaid agencies could not say](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-18-179) how many critical incidents, such as abuse or unexplained deaths, happened in the assisted living facilities they paid for.

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911.
- **Long-Term Care Ombudsman.** Every state has one. Ombudsmen take complaints from nursing home and assisted living residents and their families, and work for the resident. Find yours through the Eldercare Locator, 1-800-677-1116, or [Consumer Voice's directory](https://theconsumervoice.org/get-help/).
- **State survey agency.** Complaints about abuse, neglect, too few staff or unsafe conditions in a nursing home go to the state survey agency, usually part of the state health department. CMS lists [each state's agency](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-safety-standards/quality-safety-oversight-general-information/contact-information), or call 1-800-MEDICARE, 1-800-633-4227 (TTY 1-877-486-2048), for the contact.
- **Adult Protective Services** takes reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of older and disabled adults. Find your state's number through [NAPSA](https://www.napsa-now.org/help-in-your-area/).
- **Medicaid Fraud Control Units** investigate and prosecute [abuse and neglect of residents](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/medicaid-fraud-control-units-mfcu/) in facilities that take Medicaid.
- **Protection and Advocacy.** For disabled residents, including younger people who want to leave a nursing home, there is a [Protection and Advocacy agency](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/) in every state and territory.
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

For abuse in a youth program, see [our reporting directory](/report-abuse/).

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care](https://theconsumervoice.org/): Founded in 1975 as the National Citizens' Coalition for Nursing Home Reform; speaks for long-term care residents nationally and runs the National Long-Term Care Ombudsman Resource Center.
- [Long Term Care Community Coalition (nursinghome411)](https://nursinghome411.org/): Publishes nursing home staffing, inspection and antipsychotic data and guides for residents and families.
- [Center for Medicare Advocacy](https://medicareadvocacy.org/): A nonprofit law organization; tracks nursing home enforcement and residents' rights.
- [Justice in Aging](https://justiceinaging.org/): Legal advocacy for older adults with low incomes, including the rights of people living in nursing homes.
- [California Advocates for Nursing Home Reform](https://canhr.org/): Fact sheets, legal referrals and advocacy for people in California's long-term care facilities.
- [ADAPT](https://adapt.org/): A disability rights group, led by disabled people, that fights for the right to live at home instead of in nursing homes.
